5.8.4  Compression Specimen

For compression testing some cylindrical specimens have been produced

with L/D ratio of 1,5. The successful printed specimens will be printed 3

times to  test them and obtain mean and standard deviation of the

mechanical properties. This geometry, even if looking simple, hides some

problems due to the small area of each layer which makes these samples166





prone to the overheating problem. As mentioned in the DOE the body

temperature will always be kept 5 °C lower than the nozzle one.

Sample n. 1 with nozzle temperature of 375 and fan at 0% speed resulted in

blockage of the machine due to high viscosity of the polymer and not

enough power from the extruder motor. The result is show in Figure 146.

The drop on top of the specimen is caused by the pneumatic closure of the

nozzle which closes the orifice when an error occurs, pushing some material

out of it in an uncontrolled manner.





                                Figure 146: Compression specimen n. 1

Sample n. 2 with nozzle temperature of 380 °C and no fan (Figure 147) was

produced in the correct manner, without blocking the machine neither

problems post extrusion, even if some slight overheating on the top surface

is present. Therefore, three samples are printed for testing.                                                               167





                                Figure 147: Compression specimen n. 2

Sample number 3 with nozzle temperature of 385 °C and no fan shows signs

of overheating problem, mainly related to the geometry. Indeed, the time to

make a layer was shorter than other pieces in the experimental campaign

and the piece did not have enough time to cool due to convection. Two trials

for this condition were performed but both resulted in overheating problem

which make the geometry different from the one of the cad file, resulting in

non-testable parts, as shown in Figure 148.





                                Figure 148: Compression specimen n. 3168





Sample n. 4 with nozzle temperature of 390 °C and fan at 0% power (Figure

149) showed signs of material degradation inside the machine, due to a too

high temperature in the extruder chamber and nozzle and too slow

extrusion rate, which resulted in degraded material.





                                Figure 149: Compression specimen n. 4

Sample n. 5 with nozzle temperature of 375 °C and 25% fan speed blocked

the machine due to overload, same condition happened with sample n. 1,

since the fan speed does not affect the material prior to extrusion and the

viscosity was too high. In Figure 150 the trial is shown.





                                Figure 150: Compression specimen n. 5

Sample n. 6 with nozzle temperature of 380 °C and 25% layer fan speed was

produced in a flawless manner, without any sign of overheating, material

degradation nor delamination. The result is presented in Figure 151 .                                                               169





                                Figure 151: Compression specimen n. 6

Sample n. 7 with nozzle temperature of 385 °C and 25% layer fan speed was

produced with good shape and color, without any sign of overheating,

material degradation nor delamination. The specimens prior to testing are

presented in Figure 152 .





                                Figure 152: Compression specimen n. 7170





Sample n. 8 with nozzle temperature of 390 °C and fan at 25% power (Figure

153) showed, as for sample n. 4, signs of material degradation inside the

machine, even in this case changing the fan speed did not improve the

situation since the thermal problem was in the extruder chamber.





                                Figure 153: Compression specimen n. 8

Sample n. 9 with nozzle temperature of 375 °C and fan speed at 50% was

not printed due to the high probability of machine overload, since both the

previous trials at this temperature gave overload.

Sample n. 10 with nozzle temperature of 380 °C and layer fan speed at 50%

resulted in delamination due to too cool substrate when depositing the next

part. The process was thus interrupted. The result is shown in Figure 154.

Sample n. 11 with nozzle temperature of 385 °C and 50% layer fan power

also resulted in a delaminated specimen, shown in Figure 155, which is not

adequate for testing, therefore the printing phase was interrupted and no

more specimens with this condition were printed.





                               Figure 155: Compression specimen n. 11

Sample n. 12 with nozzle temperature of 390 °C and layer fan at 50% was

not printed since both the previous trials at this temperature resulted in

material degradation and increasing the fan speed would not have fixed

this problem.


From the printing phase of the compression specimens, it is possible to

notice how the temperature of 375 °C always gives machine blockage due

to high viscosity of the ULTEM material in the extrusion temperature and

not enough motor torque to extrude  it. On the other hand a nozzle

temperature of 390 °C always gives material degradation inside the

machine, resulting in poor material properties and aspect once extruded.172

adjusting the layer fan speed.

with 25% fan speed. The tendency to delaminate was observed even in the

staircase effect sample n. 2 and in the previous tests each geometry with

50% fan power delaminated, therefore this conclusion is straightforward.

In Table 26 the results of the staircase effect test are reported, all the

variables except the layer fan are kept constant as in Table 8.


   Staircase test          1                2                3

    Layer fan        0%           25%          50%

  Accomplished

                      Strong                           Probable
     Notes                        Adequate
                    overheating                      Delamination

                                     Table 26: Staircase test result

5.8.10 Considerations on the results obtained

From the experimental campaign carried out some final conclusions about

ULTEM printing with the EFeSTO machine can be drawn. Regarding the

layer fan the optimum has been found to be at 25%, which permits to print

in an adequate manner most of the geometries tested. For lower layer fan

speeds the overheating problem might appear, while for higher ones

delamination occurs.

Regarding the printing temperature the process window is tight, with good

results only  in  the range  of 380-385 °C nozzle temperature (Body

temperature 5 °C lower), for lower temperatures the viscosity of the

material  is too high to be extruded by the brushless motor installed,

resulting in machine overload. For higher temperatures instead material

degradations happens inside the extruder chamber.

The IR lights can be used with power lower than 50%, resulting in

overheating and material degradation if set higher. The IR preheating as                                                               195





pointed out by A. Nycz et al. [45] is useful only if the substrate temperature

falls below the glass transition temperature of the material, condition which

probably does not occur with small samples as the one printed for this

thesis. The IR preheating has been found to be effective if used during the

first layer to improve bed adhesion and prevent warping.

The bed temperature has an important role in preventing warping, giving

better results if it is set close to the material glass transition temperature,

such to have a soft material in the first layer capable of absorbing stresses

without excessive deformations.

The geometry of the specimen to be printed influences a lot the thermal

parameters to be set, since depending on the area of each layer the time to

complete a single layer might vary and thus the heat naturally dissipated

by convection and conduction. For smaller layer area the tendency to the

overheating problem increases. For increasing infill percentage the thermal

inertia of the layer will increase thus increasing the overheating tendency.

The mechanical properties of the material have been tested and the results

are satisfactory, showing how ULTEM material is a high strength material

able to withstand high loads for respect to many other thermoplastics. For

this reason it can be of interest in application where a high mechanical

resistance is required. Thanks to its high temperature resistance it can also

be used for Rapid Tooling in injection molding.


5.8.11 Comparison with ABS results

The results obtained with ULTEM and ABS are very different for the same

geometry and this can be explained by the two materials having different

thermal parameters, as shown in Table 27. Attention has to be focused on

the glass transition temperature and conductivity of the two materials.196

 Glass transition temperature [°C]      109              215

      Conductivity [W/(mK)]        0,128-0,187            0,22

         Density [g/cm3]             1,04-1,08             1,27

                             Table 27: ABS-ULTEM properties of interest

For the same geometry and fan speed ABS shows overheating in a much

more important way with respect to ULTEM. In other terms, ABS requires

a higher fan speed to avoid overheating, while ULTEM a lower fan speed

to avoid delamination. For the overhang test ABS optimum has been found

to be at 100% fan speed, with good geometry and no signs of delamination,

while for ULTEM at fan speed 25%, with delamination present at just 50%

fan speed.

These results can be explained from a thermal point of view. ABS has an

extrusion temperature much lower than ULTEM and the ambient and bed

temperature can be considered similar. Therefore, assuming a constant

convection coefficient, the heat extracted by convection will be much higher

in ULTEM printing since the gradient  is higher. Usually even heat

extraction by conduction will be higher with ULTEM material, but this

function.arguments:
{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a ranked recommendation table for PEI/ULTEM build plate surfaces, split into two scenarios:

SCENARIO A: Low-temperature printer (bed ~120°C, chamber ~65°C)
Rank 1: Borosilicate glass + PI (Kapton) tape + Magigoo HT adhesive - best compromise at limited bed temperature; Magigoo HT tolerates up to 150°C, Kapton stable, glass won't buckle. Use large brim. Expect some warpage on large parts.
Rank 2: G10/FR4 Garolite (high-Tg grade) + Magigoo HT - good surface texture for grip, but FR4 epoxy may degrade at prolonged use above 130°C. Limited lifespan.
Rank 3: PEI-coated spring steel + Magigoo HT - flex-release is convenient, but PEI coating Tg at 217°C means no fusion risk at 120°C, though adhesion will be marginal. Warpage likely.
Not recommended: Dimafix (degrades above 125°C), bare glass, bare aluminium, PVA glue stick (burns off at PEI temps).

SCENARIO B: High-temperature printer (bed 160-200°C, chamber ≥150°C)
Rank 1: Borosilicate glass + Nano Polymer Adhesive (Vision Miner) or Magigoo HT - excellent adhesion at 200°C bed, 100°C+ chamber reduces thermal gradient and warping, glass is stable and reusable, adhesive is renewable. Best for open-platform/third-party printers.
Rank 2: Borosilicate glass + PI tape + PVP adhesive - validated at 150°C bed for PEI, PI tape thermally stable to 350°C, good adhesion without risk of fusion.
Rank 3: PEI sheet + Magigoo HT at 180°C bed - no warpage at 180°C, excellent adhesion, but risk of PEI-to-PEI fusion if bed temp exceeds 200°C. Use Magigoo as barrier.
Rank 4: Stratasys Fortus/F900 (disposable build sheet + raft) - industrial gold standard with 220-225°C chamber, but proprietary and disposable. Single-use sheets add cost.
Rank 5: Sanded carbon-fibre plate at 150°C - good adhesion in initial tests, but limited data and potential for thermal expansion mismatch.
Not recommended: bare aluminium (buckles), bare glass (insufficient adhesion), Dimafix (degrades), PEI sheet without barrier adhesive at >200°C bed (fusion risk).

Include columns: Rank, Bed Surface + Treatment, Suitability Rating (1-5 stars), Key Advantage, Key Risk, Notes."}

{"answer": "# Build Plate Surface Selection for FDM/FFF 3D Printing of Polyetherimide (PEI/ULTEM)

## 1. Introduction and Scope

Achieving reliable first-layer adhesion during material-extrusion printing of polyetherimide (PEI; SABIC ULTEM 9085, T_g ≈ 186 °C, and ULTEM 1010, T_g ≈ 215–217 °C) is among the most challenging aspects of high-temperature fused filament fabrication (FFF/FDM) (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000011). The principal difficulty arises from the large thermal gradient between the extrusion temperature (typically 365–390 °C) and the bed temperature, which generates high shrinkage stresses that can detach or curl the part during printing (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000056). The ideal bed surface must therefore (i) provide strong adhesion to molten PEI during the print, (ii) allow damage-free release after cooling, (iii) tolerate continuous operation at the required bed temperature, and (iv) resist progressive wear over many print cycles.

## 2. Candidate Build Surfaces and Reported Performance

### 2.1 Borosilicate Glass with Polyimide (Kapton) Tape and PVP Adhesive

A modified high-temperature FFF printer used a 3 mm borosilicate glass build plate with PI (polyimide/Kapton-type) tape and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) adhesive at a 150 °C bed temperature (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000023). PEI adhered well, and 1 mm-thick test specimens showed no visible warping or shrinkage after cooling. This configuration was adopted after bare aluminium proved unsuitable—it buckled during heating, producing approximately 1.5 mm of edge deviation and uneven part thickness (pqac-00000000). The PI film itself has a reported T_g of approximately 348.6 °C (pqac-00000029), making it one of the most thermally robust polymeric bed surfaces. However, the pressure-sensitive adhesive backing of commercial Kapton tape typically fails well below that temperature, requiring periodic replacement.

### 2.2 Borosilicate Glass with Nano Polymer Adhesive (Vision Miner / Slice Engineering)

An open-source high-temperature printer developed for ULTEM 1010 used borosilicate glass with Vision Miner Nano Polymer Adhesive at a 200 °C bed and approximately 80–100 °C chamber temperature (pqac-00000016). A minimum of four coats of the adhesive was recommended for best results, and a brim was still needed for most parts because warpage could occur even with properly applied adhesive (pqac-00000016). The printer produced ULTEM 1010 calibration cubes (20 × 20 × 20 mm) and successful ULTEM 9085 and PEEK parts, confirming the suitability of this glass-plus-adhesive approach at high bed temperatures. The printer's heated bed could reach 200 °C and its chamber heater 120 °C (pqac-00000016).

### 2.3 PEI (ULTEM) Sheet with Magigoo HT Adhesive

Magigoo HT, a commercial adhesive engineered for high-temperature polymers (PEEK, PEKK, PEI), was tested on a PEI build sheet for ULTEM 1000 printing at bed temperatures of 120, 150, and 180 °C (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000056). The results were as follows:

- **120 °C bed**: Significant warping across the entire specimen; the adhesive and 10 mm brim were insufficient to keep the part flat, and warping began during deposition of the first layer (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056).
- **150 °C bed**: Dramatic improvement, with only slight warping at the extreme edges of the part, occurring mainly upon removal from the build surface due to residual stresses. During printing, adhesion was adequate and no warping occurred (pqac-00000056).
- **180 °C bed**: The part adhered perfectly with no significant warping, either during printing or after removal (pqac-00000056).

Magigoo HT provided adequate adhesion for complex and elongated geometries including tensile test specimens, where a previous attempt with Dimafix had failed (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043).

### 2.4 PEI Sheet with Dimafix Spray — Not Recommended

Dimafix spray adhesive, while effective for ABS at 120 °C bed temperature, degraded and lost its adhesive properties above approximately 125 °C (pqac-00000041). When used for ULTEM printing at 125 °C, it could not restrain high-shrinkage geometries such as tensile specimens, though shorter compression cylinders were successful. The limitation was attributed to the high thermal stresses generated by ULTEM's large extrusion-to-bed temperature gradient (350–400 °C vs. 125 °C) exceeding Dimafix's adhesive capacity (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043).

### 2.5 Sanded Carbon-Fibre Composite Plate

Initial PEI printing trials on a sanded 1.5 mm carbon-fibre surface at a 150 °C bed temperature showed good adhesion, with 1 mm-thick specimens exhibiting no visible warping or shrinkage after cooling (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). However, the aluminium base plate supporting this surface buckled during heating, motivating the switch to borosilicate glass. The carbon-fibre surface's performance was validated only for thin parts, and no removal-force, wear, or lifetime data were reported.

### 2.6 PEI-Coated Spring Steel

Adhesion testing with PETG (not ULTEM) on PEI-coated spring steel yielded a mean maximum tear-off force of 53.48 ± 7.95 N, compared with only 33.09 ± 5.52 N on uncoated aluminium (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000026). The flexible spring steel sheet can be bent to aid part release after cooling. However, these measurements were performed with PETG at 85 °C and cannot be directly extrapolated to ULTEM at 150–200 °C. The PEI coating's T_g (~217 °C for ULTEM 1010) means that at high bed temperatures approaching or exceeding this value, the coating itself may soften and bond to the printed part, posing a fusion risk.

### 2.7 Bare Aluminium — Not Recommended

Aluminium exhibited thermal expansion problems at the temperatures required for PEI printing. A thin aluminium heated bed buckled during heating to 150 °C, producing approximately 1.5 mm of edge deviation and uneven part thickness (pqac-00000000). Additionally, bare aluminium showed the lowest adhesion force in comparative testing (33.09 N mean for PETG) (pqac-00000026).

### 2.8 Bare Borosilicate Glass — Insufficient Without Adhesive

Smooth bare borosilicate glass was found to lose adhesion after the first few prints of a high-temperature thermoplastic polyimide; a PEI bed with nano polymer adhesive was subsequently adopted to address this problem (pqac-00000005). Similarly, PI tape and PVP adhesive were applied to glass because the smooth surface alone was insufficient for PEI adhesion (pqac-00000002).

### 2.9 Stratasys Fortus/F900 Industrial Systems

Stratasys Fortus 450mc and F900 systems, the primary industrial platforms for ULTEM 9085 and 1010, employ maximum active-convection chamber temperatures of ≤220 °C and ≤225 °C, respectively (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000033). These systems use dual extrusion with breakaway or soluble support materials, and parts are printed on disposable build sheets with a machine-generated support-material foundation (raft) that mediates adhesion and release. While this approach is industrially validated and qualified for aerospace applications, the specific build sheet composition and bed temperature setpoints were not disclosed in the reviewed literature (pqac-00000027). The disposable single-use build sheet avoids cumulative surface damage but adds per-build consumable cost.

### 2.10 G10/FR4 Garolite

G10/FR4 glass-epoxy laminate is mentioned in the context of large-format additive manufacturing systems, but no controlled ULTEM adhesion-force, release, or lifetime data were located in the reviewed literature. The principal concern is the limited thermal capability of the epoxy matrix: standard FR4 grades have T_g values in the 130–180 °C range, and prolonged exposure to PEI printing bed temperatures (150–200 °C) can cause discolouration, warping, or delamination of the laminate.

### 2.11 PEEK and PPSU Sheets

No controlled build-plate adhesion data for ULTEM printed on PEEK or PPSU sheets were identified in the reviewed literature. PEEK (T_g ≈ 143 °C, continuous use up to ~250 °C) and PPSU (T_g ≈ 220 °C) are thermally compatible candidates, and their immiscibility with PEI might reduce fusion risk relative to a PEI-on-PEI configuration. However, without published adhesion or release data, their ranking remains speculative.

## 3. The Role of Bed and Chamber Temperature

The fundamental finding from warpage studies is that bed temperature is the dominant factor controlling first-layer adhesion and warpage for PEI printing. The general principle established for FFF adhesion—that optimal adhesion occurs at a bed temperature slightly above the glass transition temperature of the printing material (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030)—implies that PEI ideally requires a bed temperature of approximately 190–220 °C (above T_g) for best adhesion and minimum warpage. At 120 °C, significant warping occurred in all ULTEM specimens tested; at 150 °C, warping was dramatically reduced; and at 180 °C, warping was eliminated (pqac-00000056).

Chamber temperature provides a secondary but important benefit. A heated chamber reduces the thermal gradient between deposited layers and the environment, thereby reducing residual stresses. Increasing the heated chamber temperature from ambient to 120 °C produced a 36% reduction in warpage RMSD for PEI samples, though approximately 1 mm of deflection remained at specimen extremities (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054). PEI nozzle temperatures typically range from 355–390 °C, with bed temperatures of 120–160 °C and a heated chamber recommended (pqac-00000003).

## 4. Comprehensive Build Surface Comparison

The following table summarizes the reported performance of each candidate build surface for PEI/ULTEM printing:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## 5. Ranked Recommendations

The recommendations are separated by printer capability, as the available bed and chamber temperatures fundamentally constrain the achievable adhesion and warpage control:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

## 6. Summary and Conclusions

**For high-temperature printers (bed 160–200 °C, chamber ≥150 °C):** The best-supported approach is **borosilicate glass with a high-temperature adhesive** (Vision Miner Nano Polymer Adhesive or Magigoo HT), operated at the highest available bed temperature (ideally 180–200 °C). This combination provides strong adhesion without the risk of same-material fusion, the glass is dimensionally stable and reusable, and the adhesive coating is renewable. This was validated for ULTEM 1010 at a 200 °C bed (pqac-00000016) and for ULTEM 1000 at 150–180 °C with Magigoo HT (pqac-00000056). Alternatively, borosilicate glass with PI tape and PVP adhesive is validated at 150 °C (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000023) and offers a thermally robust interface. A PEI sheet with Magigoo HT is effective, particularly at 180 °C where warpage was eliminated (pqac-00000056), but users should be aware of the PEI-to-PEI fusion risk at higher temperatures.

**For temperature-limited printers (bed ~120 °C, chamber ~65 °C):** Printing PEI at these temperatures is inherently challenging because 120 °C is far below the T_g of either ULTEM grade. Significant warpage was documented at a 120 °C bed even with adhesive and brim (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056). The best compromise is **borosilicate glass with PI tape and Magigoo HT**, combined with a large brim (10–20 mm), slow first-layer speed (10 mm/s), and infrared preheating of the first layer if available (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043). Users should expect partial warpage on larger parts and should consider printing only small or geometrically forgiving parts at this limited bed temperature.

**Surfaces to avoid for PEI printing** include bare aluminium (thermal distortion), bare borosilicate glass without adhesive (insufficient grip), Dimafix spray (degrades above ~125 °C), and uncoated PEI sheets at bed temperatures above ~200 °C (fusion risk). Standard PVA glue sticks are not rated for the temperatures involved and should not be used.
"}

### 2.1 Borosilicate Glass with Polyimide (Kapton) Tape and PVP Adhesive

A modified high-temperature FFF printer used a 3 mm borosilicate glass build plate with PI (polyimide/Kapton-type) tape and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) adhesive at a 150 °C bed temperature (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000023). This configuration was adopted after bare aluminium proved unsuitable—it buckled during heating, producing approximately 1.5 mm of edge deviation and uneven part thickness (pqac-00000000). The PI film itself has a reported T_g of approximately 348.6 °C (pqac-00000029), making it one of the most thermally robust polymeric bed surfaces. However, the pressure-sensitive adhesive backing of commercial Kapton tape typically fails well below that temperature, requiring periodic replacement.

### 2.2 Borosilicate Glass with Nano Polymer Adhesive (Vision Miner / Slice Engineering)

An open-source high-temperature printer developed for ULTEM 1010 used borosilicate glass with Vision Miner Nano Polymer Adhesive at a 200 °C bed and approximately 80–100 °C chamber temperature (pqac-00000016). A minimum of four coats of the adhesive was recommended for best results, and a brim was still needed for most parts because warpage could occur even with properly applied adhesive (pqac-00000016). The printer produced ULTEM 1010 calibration cubes (20 × 20 × 20 mm) and successful ULTEM 9085 and PEEK parts, confirming the suitability of this glass-plus-adhesive approach at high bed temperatures. The printer's heated bed could reach 200 °C and its chamber heater 120 °C (pqac-00000016).

### 2.3 PEI (ULTEM) Sheet with Magigoo HT Adhesive

Magigoo HT, a commercial adhesive engineered for high-temperature polymers (PEEK, PEKK, PEI), was tested on a PEI build sheet for ULTEM 1000 printing at bed temperatures of 120, 150, and 180 °C (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000056). The results were as follows:

- **120 °C bed**: Significant warping across the entire specimen; the adhesive and 10 mm brim were insufficient to keep the part flat, and warping began during deposition of the first layer (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056).
- **150 °C bed**: Dramatic improvement, with only slight warping at the extreme edges of the part, occurring mainly upon removal from the build surface due to residual stresses. During printing, adhesion was adequate and no warping occurred (pqac-00000056).
- **180 °C bed**: The part adhered perfectly with no significant warping, either during printing or after removal (pqac-00000056).

Magigoo HT provided adequate adhesion for complex and elongated geometries including tensile test specimens, where a previous attempt with Dimafix had failed (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043).

### 2.4 PEI Sheet with Dimafix Spray — Not Recommended

Dimafix spray adhesive, while effective for ABS at 120 °C bed temperature, degraded and lost its adhesive properties above approximately 125 °C (pqac-00000041). When used for ULTEM printing at 125 °C, it could not restrain high-shrinkage geometries such as tensile specimens, though shorter compression cylinders were successful. The limitation was attributed to the high thermal stresses generated by ULTEM's large extrusion-to-bed temperature gradient (350–400 °C vs. 125 °C) exceeding Dimafix's adhesive capacity (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043).

Initial PEI printing trials on a sanded 1.5 mm carbon-fibre surface at a 150 °C bed temperature showed good adhesion, with 1 mm-thick specimens exhibiting no visible warping or shrinkage after cooling (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). However, the aluminium base plate supporting this surface buckled during heating, motivating the switch to borosilicate glass. The carbon-fibre surface's performance was validated only for thin parts, and no removal-force, wear, or lifetime data were reported.

### 2.6 PEI-Coated Spring Steel

However, these measurements were performed with PETG at 85 °C and cannot be directly extrapolated to ULTEM at 150–200 °C. The PEI coating's T_g (~217 °C for ULTEM 1010) means that at high bed temperatures approaching or exceeding this value, the coating itself may soften and bond to the printed part, posing a fusion risk.

### 2.7 Bare Aluminium — Not Recommended

Aluminium exhibited thermal expansion problems at the temperatures required for PEI printing. A thin aluminium heated bed buckled during heating to 150 °C, producing approximately 1.5 mm of edge deviation and uneven part thickness (pqac-00000000). Additionally, bare aluminium showed the lowest adhesion force in comparative testing (33.09 N mean for PETG) (pqac-00000026).

### 2.8 Bare Borosilicate Glass — Insufficient Without Adhesive

Smooth bare borosilicate glass was found to lose adhesion after the first few prints of a high-temperature thermoplastic polyimide; a PEI bed with nano polymer adhesive was subsequently adopted to address this problem (pqac-00000005). Similarly, PI tape and PVP adhesive were applied to glass because the smooth surface alone was insufficient for PEI adhesion (pqac-00000002).

### 2.9 Stratasys Fortus/F900 Industrial Systems

Stratasys Fortus 450mc and F900 systems, the primary industrial platforms for ULTEM 9085 and 1010, employ maximum active-convection chamber temperatures of ≤220 °C and ≤225 °C, respectively (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000033). These systems use dual extrusion with breakaway or soluble support materials, and parts are printed on disposable build sheets with a machine-generated support-material foundation (raft) that mediates adhesion and release. While this approach is industrially validated and qualified for aerospace applications, the specific build sheet composition and bed temperature setpoints were not disclosed in the reviewed literature (pqac-00000027). The disposable single-use build sheet avoids cumulative surface damage but adds per-build consumable cost.

### 2.10 G10/FR4 Garolite

G10/FR4 glass-epoxy laminate is mentioned in the context of large-format additive manufacturing systems, but no controlled ULTEM adhesion-force, release, or lifetime data were located in the reviewed literature. The principal concern is the limited thermal capability of the epoxy matrix: standard FR4 grades have T_g values in the 130–180 °C range, and prolonged exposure to PEI printing bed temperatures (150–200 °C) can cause discolouration, warping, or delamination of the laminate.

### 2.11 PEEK and PPSU Sheets

No controlled build-plate adhesion data for ULTEM printed on PEEK or PPSU sheets were identified in the reviewed literature. PEEK (T_g ≈ 143 °C, continuous use up to ~250 °C) and PPSU (T_g ≈ 220 °C) are thermally compatible candidates, and their immiscibility with PEI might reduce fusion risk relative to a PEI-on-PEI configuration. However, without published adhesion or release data, their ranking remains speculative.

## 3. The Role of Bed and Chamber Temperature

The fundamental finding from warpage studies is that bed temperature is the dominant factor controlling first-layer adhesion and warpage for PEI printing. Increasing the heated chamber temperature from ambient to 120 °C produced a 36% reduction in warpage RMSD for PEI samples, though approximately 1 mm of deflection remained at specimen extremities (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054). PEI nozzle temperatures typically range from 355–390 °C, with bed temperatures of 120–160 °C and a heated chamber recommended (pqac-00000003).

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

This combination provides strong adhesion without the risk of same-material fusion, the glass is dimensionally stable and reusable, and the adhesive coating is renewable. **For temperature-limited printers (bed ~120 °C, chamber ~65 °C):** Printing PEI at these temperatures is inherently challenging because 120 °C is far below the T_g of either ULTEM grade. Significant warpage was documented at a 120 °C bed even with adhesive and brim (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056). **For high-temperature printers (bed 160–200 °C, chamber ≥150 °C):** The best-supported approach is **borosilicate glass with a high-temperature adhesive** (Vision Miner Nano Polymer Adhesive or Magigoo HT), operated at the highest available bed temperature (ideally 180–200 °C). This combination provides strong adhesion without the risk of same-material fusion, the glass is dimensionally stable and reusable, and the adhesive coating is renewable. This was validated for ULTEM 1010 at a 200 °C bed (thompson2026designanddevelopment pages 16-18) and for ULTEM 1000 at 150–180 °C with Magigoo HT (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 215-223). Alternatively, borosilicate glass with PI tape and PVP adhesive is validated at 150 °C (shuttleworth2020adigitalmanufacturing pages 71-75) and offers a thermally robust interface. A PEI sheet with Magigoo HT is effective, particularly at 180 °C where warpage was eliminated (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 215-223), but users should be aware of the PEI-to-PEI fusion risk at higher temperatures.

**For temperature-limited printers (bed ~120 °C, chamber ~65 °C):** Printing PEI at these temperatures is inherently challenging because 120 °C is far below the T_g of either ULTEM grade. Significant warpage was documented at a 120 °C bed even with adhesive and brim (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 209-215, fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 215-223). The best compromise is **borosilicate glass with PI tape and Magigoo HT**, combined with a large brim (10–20 mm), slow first-layer speed (10 mm/s), and infrared preheating of the first layer if available (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 158-166, fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 174-181). Users should expect partial warpage on larger parts and should consider printing only small or geometrically forgiving parts at this limited bed temperature.

**Surfaces to avoid for PEI printing** include bare aluminium (thermal distortion), bare borosilicate glass without adhesive (insufficient grip), Dimafix spray (degrades above ~125 °C), and uncoated PEI sheets at bed temperatures above ~200 °C (fusion risk). Standard PVA glue sticks are not rated for the temperatures involved and should not be used.

# Build Plate Surface Selection for FDM/FFF 3D Printing of Polyetherimide (PEI/ULTEM)

## 1. Introduction and Scope

Achieving reliable first-layer adhesion during material-extrusion printing of polyetherimide (PEI; SABIC ULTEM 9085, T_g ≈ 186 °C, and ULTEM 1010, T_g ≈ 215–217 °C) is among the most challenging aspects of high-temperature fused filament fabrication (FFF/FDM) (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000011). The principal difficulty arises from the large thermal gradient between the extrusion temperature (typically 365–390 °C) and the bed temperature, which generates high shrinkage stresses that can detach or curl the part during printing (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000056). The ideal bed surface must therefore (i) provide strong adhesion to molten PEI during the print, (ii) allow damage-free release after cooling, (iii) tolerate continuous operation at the required bed temperature, and (iv) resist progressive wear over many print cycles.

## 2. Candidate Build Surfaces and Reported Performance

### 2.1 Borosilicate Glass with Polyimide (Kapton) Tape and PVP Adhesive

A modified high-temperature FFF printer used a 3 mm borosilicate glass build plate with PI (polyimide/Kapton-type) tape and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) adhesive at a 150 °C bed temperature (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000023). PEI adhered well, and 1 mm-thick test specimens showed no visible warping or shrinkage after cooling. This configuration was adopted after bare aluminium proved unsuitable—it buckled during heating, producing approximately 1.5 mm of edge deviation and uneven part thickness (pqac-00000000). The PI film itself has a reported T_g of approximately 348.6 °C (pqac-00000029), making it one of the most thermally robust polymeric bed surfaces. However, the pressure-sensitive adhesive backing of commercial Kapton tape typically fails well below that temperature, requiring periodic replacement.

### 2.2 Borosilicate Glass with Nano Polymer Adhesive (Vision Miner / Slice Engineering)

An open-source high-temperature printer developed for ULTEM 1010 used borosilicate glass with Vision Miner Nano Polymer Adhesive at a 200 °C bed and approximately 80–100 °C chamber temperature (pqac-00000016). A minimum of four coats of the adhesive was recommended for best results, and a brim was still needed for most parts because warpage could occur even with properly applied adhesive (pqac-00000016). The printer produced ULTEM 1010 calibration cubes (20 × 20 × 20 mm) and successful ULTEM 9085 and PEEK parts, confirming the suitability of this glass-plus-adhesive approach at high bed temperatures. The printer's heated bed could reach 200 °C and its chamber heater 120 °C (pqac-00000016).

### 2.3 PEI (ULTEM) Sheet with Magigoo HT Adhesive

Magigoo HT, a commercial adhesive engineered for high-temperature polymers (PEEK, PEKK, PEI), was tested on a PEI build sheet for ULTEM 1000 printing at bed temperatures of 120, 150, and 180 °C (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000056). The results were as follows:

- **120 °C bed**: Significant warping across the entire specimen; the adhesive and 10 mm brim were insufficient to keep the part flat, and warping began during deposition of the first layer (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056).
- **150 °C bed**: Dramatic improvement, with only slight warping at the extreme edges of the part, occurring mainly upon removal from the build surface due to residual stresses. During printing, adhesion was adequate and no warping occurred (pqac-00000056).
- **180 °C bed**: The part adhered perfectly with no significant warping, either during printing or after removal (pqac-00000056).

Magigoo HT provided adequate adhesion for complex and elongated geometries including tensile test specimens, where a previous attempt with Dimafix had failed (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043).

### 2.4 PEI Sheet with Dimafix Spray — Not Recommended

Dimafix spray adhesive, while effective for ABS at 120 °C bed temperature, degraded and lost its adhesive properties above approximately 125 °C (pqac-00000041). When used for ULTEM printing at 125 °C, it could not restrain high-shrinkage geometries such as tensile specimens, though shorter compression cylinders were successful. The limitation was attributed to the high thermal stresses generated by ULTEM's large extrusion-to-bed temperature gradient (350–400 °C vs. 125 °C) exceeding Dimafix's adhesive capacity (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043).

### 2.5 Sanded Carbon-Fibre Composite Plate

Initial PEI printing trials on a sanded 1.5 mm carbon-fibre surface at a 150 °C bed temperature showed good adhesion, with 1 mm-thick specimens exhibiting no visible warping or shrinkage after cooling (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). However, the aluminium base plate supporting this surface buckled during heating, motivating the switch to borosilicate glass. The carbon-fibre surface's performance was validated only for thin parts, and no removal-force, wear, or lifetime data were reported.

### 2.6 PEI-Coated Spring Steel

Adhesion testing with PETG (not ULTEM) on PEI-coated spring steel yielded a mean maximum tear-off force of 53.48 ± 7.95 N, compared with only 33.09 ± 5.52 N on uncoated aluminium (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000026). The flexible spring steel sheet can be bent to aid part release after cooling. However, these measurements were performed with PETG at 85 °C and cannot be directly extrapolated to ULTEM at 150–200 °C. The PEI coating's T_g (~217 °C for ULTEM 1010) means that at high bed temperatures approaching or exceeding this value, the coating itself may soften and bond to the printed part, posing a fusion risk.

### 2.7 Bare Aluminium — Not Recommended

Aluminium exhibited thermal expansion problems at the temperatures required for PEI printing. A thin aluminium heated bed buckled during heating to 150 °C, producing approximately 1.5 mm of edge deviation and uneven part thickness (pqac-00000000). Additionally, bare aluminium showed the lowest adhesion force in comparative testing (33.09 N mean for PETG) (pqac-00000026).

### 2.8 Bare Borosilicate Glass — Insufficient Without Adhesive

Smooth bare borosilicate glass was found to lose adhesion after the first few prints of a high-temperature thermoplastic polyimide; a PEI bed with nano polymer adhesive was subsequently adopted to address this problem (pqac-00000005). Similarly, PI tape and PVP adhesive were applied to glass because the smooth surface alone was insufficient for PEI adhesion (pqac-00000002).

### 2.9 Stratasys Fortus/F900 Industrial Systems

Stratasys Fortus 450mc and F900 systems, the primary industrial platforms for ULTEM 9085 and 1010, employ maximum active-convection chamber temperatures of ≤220 °C and ≤225 °C, respectively (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000033). These systems use dual extrusion with breakaway or soluble support materials, and parts are printed on disposable build sheets with a machine-generated support-material foundation (raft) that mediates adhesion and release. While this approach is industrially validated and qualified for aerospace applications, the specific build sheet composition and bed temperature setpoints were not disclosed in the reviewed literature (pqac-00000027). The disposable single-use build sheet avoids cumulative surface damage but adds per-build consumable cost.

### 2.10 G10/FR4 Garolite

G10/FR4 glass-epoxy laminate is mentioned in the context of large-format additive manufacturing systems, but no controlled ULTEM adhesion-force, release, or lifetime data were located in the reviewed literature. The principal concern is the limited thermal capability of the epoxy matrix: standard FR4 grades have T_g values in the 130–180 °C range, and prolonged exposure to PEI printing bed temperatures (150–200 °C) can cause discolouration, warping, or delamination of the laminate.

### 2.11 PEEK and PPSU Sheets

No controlled build-plate adhesion data for ULTEM printed on PEEK or PPSU sheets were identified in the reviewed literature. PEEK (T_g ≈ 143 °C, continuous use up to ~250 °C) and PPSU (T_g ≈ 220 °C) are thermally compatible candidates, and their immiscibility with PEI might reduce fusion risk relative to a PEI-on-PEI configuration. However, without published adhesion or release data, their ranking remains speculative.

## 3. The Role of Bed and Chamber Temperature

The fundamental finding from warpage studies is that bed temperature is the dominant factor controlling first-layer adhesion and warpage for PEI printing. The general principle established for FFF adhesion—that optimal adhesion occurs at a bed temperature slightly above the glass transition temperature of the printing material (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030)—implies that PEI ideally requires a bed temperature of approximately 190–220 °C (above T_g) for best adhesion and minimum warpage. At 120 °C, significant warping occurred in all ULTEM specimens tested; at 150 °C, warping was dramatically reduced; and at 180 °C, warping was eliminated (pqac-00000056).

Chamber temperature provides a secondary but important benefit. A heated chamber reduces the thermal gradient between deposited layers and the environment, thereby reducing residual stresses. Increasing the heated chamber temperature from ambient to 120 °C produced a 36% reduction in warpage RMSD for PEI samples, though approximately 1 mm of deflection remained at specimen extremities (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054). PEI nozzle temperatures typically range from 355–390 °C, with bed temperatures of 120–160 °C and a heated chamber recommended (pqac-00000003).

Fortus 450mc and F900 chamber limits are ≤220°C and ≤225°C respectively; these are machine limits, not confirmed ULTEM setpoints (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000033) |

*Table: Ranked build-surface recommendations for temperature-limited and industrial high-temperature PEI/ULTEM printers. Ratings distinguish directly reported results from engineering extrapolations and identify important release and surface-damage risks.*

## 6. Summary and Conclusions

**For high-temperature printers (bed 160–200 °C, chamber ≥150 °C):** The best-supported approach is **borosilicate glass with a high-temperature adhesive** (Vision Miner Nano Polymer Adhesive or Magigoo HT), operated at the highest available bed temperature (ideally 180–200 °C). This combination provides strong adhesion without the risk of same-material fusion, the glass is dimensionally stable and reusable, and the adhesive coating is renewable. This was validated for ULTEM 1010 at a 200 °C bed (pqac-00000016) and for ULTEM 1000 at 150–180 °C with Magigoo HT (pqac-00000056). Alternatively, borosilicate glass with PI tape and PVP adhesive is validated at 150 °C (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000023) and offers a thermally robust interface. A PEI sheet with Magigoo HT is effective, particularly at 180 °C where warpage was eliminated (pqac-00000056), but users should be aware of the PEI-to-PEI fusion risk at higher temperatures.

**For temperature-limited printers (bed ~120 °C, chamber ~65 °C):** Printing PEI at these temperatures is inherently challenging because 120 °C is far below the T_g of either ULTEM grade. Significant warpage was documented at a 120 °C bed even with adhesive and brim (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056). The best compromise is **borosilicate glass with PI tape and Magigoo HT**, combined with a large brim (10–20 mm), slow first-layer speed (10 mm/s), and infrared preheating of the first layer if available (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043). Users should expect partial warpage on larger parts and should consider printing only small or geometrically forgiving parts at this limited bed temperature.

**Surfaces to avoid for PEI printing** include bare aluminium (thermal distortion), bare borosilicate glass without adhesive (insufficient grip), Dimafix spray (degrades above ~125 °C), and uncoated PEI sheets at bed temperatures above ~200 °C (fusion risk). Standard PVA glue sticks are not rated for the temperatures involved and should not be used.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a customized high-temperature FFF printer used for PEI (ULTEM) printing, rather than Apium, Intamsys, 3DGence, AON3D, or Miniaturefactory machines specifically. Initial PEI trials used a 1.5 mm sanded carbon-fiber print surface. With a nozzle temperature of 365 °C and bed temperature of 150 °C, the PEI adhered well to that surface, and the 1 mm test parts showed no visible warping or shrinkage after cooling. Because the aluminum bed buckled under heating, the setup was changed to slotted mounts and a 3 mm borosilicate-glass sheet. Since the glass was smooth, the manufacturer-recommended adhesion system was PI (polyimide) tape coated with polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) adhesive. The modified bed could reach 200 °C peak and operate continuously at 150 °C; the reported PEI print configuration used a 150 °C bed. No chamber temperature is given in this excerpt. It also does not report use of a PEI bed sheet, PEI-to-PEI fusion, or comparative bed surfaces/adhesives for the named commercial printers.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not compare build-plate materials, adhesion, release, warpage, temperatures, or surface lifetimes. It studies ULTEM 9085/9085CF thermal stability and microstructure. In air, 5% mass-loss temperatures were **496 °C** (9085) and **562 °C** (9085CF); degradation inflections occurred near **570–580 °C**, with PEI expected to fully degrade around **700 °C**. A 14-layer part showed strongest lateral expansion in layer 1, some in layer 2, and poor upper-layer adhesion/crevices above layer 8. Alternating 9085/9085CF produced **~16% overall porosity** (ABABAB) versus **~29%** (AAABBB).

contexts.context: The excerpt does not identify Dimafix, Magigoo, Nano Polymer Adhesive, or any other separate bed adhesive for ULTEM/PEI 3D printing. It evaluates bed surfaces rather than adhesive products, including spring steel with a PEI coating. The reported tests concern PETG models, not ULTEM parts. In Table 4, the spring-steel PEI surface required a mean maximum tear-off force of 53.48 N, compared with 33.09 N for an uncoated pure-aluminum sheet; the corresponding standard deviations were 7.95 N and 5.52 N. Thus, within this experiment, the PEI-coated spring-steel surface exhibited substantially greater measured adhesion than uncoated aluminum. The excerpt describes removal as detaching or tearing the printed model from the build plate while measuring the maximum force, but it does not specify a particular manual removal technique, such as flexing the spring steel, scraping, or applying heat. A temperature of 85 °C is explicitly shown for the tempered glass with PI layer and borosilicate glass comparison in Figure 5, but no print-bed temperature is provided here for the PEI-coated spring-steel tests. Therefore, the excerpt supports identifying the surface as PEI-coated spring steel and provides adhesion-force results, but it does not establish the adhesive brand, ULTEM-specific performance, or PEI-bed operating temperature.

contexts.context: For ULTEM/PEI printing, the excerpt identifies polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) adhesive—not Dimafix, Magigoo, or Nano Polymer Adhesive—used together with a layer of PI (Kapton-type) tape. The final bed surface was 3 mm thick borosilicate glass, replacing the initially used sanded carbon-fibre surface. The bed was operated at 150 °C; the upgraded heater could reach 200 °C, with 150 °C specified as its continuous operating temperature. In initial tests at a 365 °C nozzle temperature and 150 °C bed temperature, PEI adhered well to the sanded carbon-fibre surface, and 1 mm-thick samples showed no warping or shrinkage after removal and cooling. The original aluminium bed buckled under heating, causing approximately 1.5 mm of edge deviation and uneven thickness. Slotted mounts and borosilicate glass resolved this thermal-expansion problem. Because the glass was smooth, PI tape and PVP adhesive were added to improve adhesion. The resulting setup had minimal warp and a 150 mm square printable area. The excerpt does not provide a specific removal procedure beyond stating that parts were removed after cooling, nor does it compare adhesive performance against Dimafix, Magigoo, or Nano Polymer Adhesive.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not identify Dimafix, Magigoo, or Nano Polymer Adhesive, and it does not specifically discuss ULTEM/PEI filament. It does, however, compare glass with a PI (polyimide) bed surface. For ABS, the authors report that PI provides substantially better adhesion than glass and conclude that a PI bed with a temperature of at least 120°C, above the material’s glass-transition temperature, is needed to ensure proper adhesion for larger parts. The study describes adhesion as increasing strongly and nonlinearly with bed temperature, while noting that excessive adhesion can damage the bed during cooling. For removal, ABS adhesion to both PI and glass is already negligible at approximately 50°C, so parts can be removed easily at a slightly elevated temperature. The paper’s quantitative recommendations are for ABS and PLA, not ULTEM PEI; therefore, these findings should not be treated as a validated adhesive, surface, or temperature specification for ULTEM. The excerpt supports PI as a studied bed surface and temperature-dependent adhesion behavior, but provides no evidence for which commercial bed adhesive should be used or whether an adhesive is required.

Instead, for ULTEM/PEI printing it reports using a 3 mm borosilicate glass bed with a layer of PI (polyimide) tape and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) adhesive, following the PEI manufacturer’s advice. contexts.context: The excerpt reports adhesion testing of printed PLA and ABS strands on glass and 0.05-mm polyimide (PI) film, using a shearing block/load cell and 16 strands per setting. Adhesion rose with bed temperature through 60–70°C; above 70°C, forces generally fell to “roughly 50–60%” of the 70°C value, attributed to fingering/Saffman–Taylor instabilities. PI showed continued adhesion increase from 80–100°C because polymer segment mobility increased, but measurements stopped above 100°C when the adhesive attaching PI to glass failed. Thus, PI-film durability and attachment—not merely adhesion—are critical limitations.

contexts.context: Spoerk et al. state that first-layer adhesion must be high enough to prevent shifting, warping, and delamination, yet low enough for nondestructive part/bed separation. Recommended approaches include cleaning and leveling, polymer films (e.g., polyimide tape), roughening, glues/coatings, same-material plates, cleated surfaces, and elevated bed temperature. It does provide general guidance about high-temperature bed adhesion. Adhesion rises strongly as the bed temperature approaches and exceeds the printed polymer’s glass-transition temperature (TG), but excessively high adhesion can damage the bed during cooling. For the materials studied, ABS required at least 120°C and a PI (polyimide) bed surface for reliable adhesion, while PLA required temperatures above 60°C regardless of whether the surface was glass or PI. The authors recommend selecting a moderate adhesion range rather than maximizing adhesion. They report that PLA on glass may adhere so strongly at 70°C that removal damage becomes a concern, whereas near-room-temperature printing facilitates damage-free removal. The excerpt therefore supports only broad comparisons involving glass and PI surfaces and temperature-dependent adhesion; it does not establish the appropriate bed temperature, surface, or clean-release behavior for ULTEM PEI with Dimafix or Magigoo products.

Question: For material-extrusion (FFF/FDM) 3D printing of polyetherimide (PEI; SABIC ULTEM 9085 and ULTEM 1010 filament, Tg about 186 C and 217 C), which build plate (print bed) material and surface treatment gives the best first-layer adhesion during printing combined with clean, damage-free part release afterwards? Compare the candidate bed surfaces reported in the literature and in printer and material-supplier documentation: polyimide (Kapton) film or tape on glass or aluminium; borosilicate glass, bare or with adhesives (PVA glue stick, PEI/ULTEM dissolved in solvent as a slurry, commercial high-temperature adhesives such as Magigoo PEEK/PEI or Vision Miner Nano Polymer Adhesive); smooth or textured PEI (ULTEM) sheets, including the risk of a PEI part fusing to a PEI bed; G10/FR4 glass-epoxy (Garolite); PEEK or polysulfone/PPSU sheets; the high-temperature build sheets and support-material rafts used by Stratasys Fortus/F900 printers for ULTEM 9085 and ULTEM 1010; carbon-fibre composite plates; and bare or coated metal (aluminium, spring steel, steel with a PEI coating). For each surface report the bed and chamber temperatures used, measured adhesion force or warpage/curling, removal behaviour, surface wear or degradation and lifetime, and the maximum continuous-use temperature of the surface itself. Conclude with a ranked recommendation, and state separately what works best when the printer's bed is limited to about 120 C and its chamber to about 65 C, versus a printer with a 160-200 C bed and a heated chamber at 150 C or more.

# Build Plate Surface Selection for FDM/FFF 3D Printing of Polyetherimide (PEI/ULTEM)

## 1. Introduction and Scope

Achieving reliable first-layer adhesion during material-extrusion printing of polyetherimide (PEI; SABIC ULTEM 9085, T_g ≈ 186 °C, and ULTEM 1010, T_g ≈ 215–217 °C) is among the most challenging aspects of high-temperature fused filament fabrication (FFF/FDM) (loh2020anoverviewof pages 4-5, fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 26-32). The principal difficulty arises from the large thermal gradient between the extrusion temperature (typically 365–390 °C) and the bed temperature, which generates high shrinkage stresses that can detach or curl the part during printing (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 158-166, fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 215-223). The ideal bed surface must therefore (i) provide strong adhesion to molten PEI during the print, (ii) allow damage-free release after cooling, (iii) tolerate continuous operation at the required bed temperature, and (iv) resist progressive wear over many print cycles.

## 2. Candidate Build Surfaces and Reported Performance

### 2.1 Borosilicate Glass with Polyimide (Kapton) Tape and PVP Adhesive

A modified high-temperature FFF printer used a 3 mm borosilicate glass build plate with PI (polyimide/Kapton-type) tape and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) adhesive at a 150 °C bed temperature (shuttleworth2020adigitalmanufacturing pages 71-75). PEI adhered well, and 1 mm-thick test specimens showed no visible warping or shrinkage after cooling. This configuration was adopted after bare aluminium proved unsuitable—it buckled during heating, producing approximately 1.5 mm of edge deviation and uneven part thickness (shuttleworth2020adigitalmanufacturing pages 71-75). The PI film itself has a reported T_g of approximately 348.6 °C (spoerk2018effectofthe pages 3-4), making it one of the most thermally robust polymeric bed surfaces. However, the pressure-sensitive adhesive backing of commercial Kapton tape typically fails well below that temperature, requiring periodic replacement.

### 2.2 Borosilicate Glass with Nano Polymer Adhesive (Vision Miner / Slice Engineering)

An open-source high-temperature printer developed for ULTEM 1010 used borosilicate glass with Vision Miner Nano Polymer Adhesive at a 200 °C bed and approximately 80–100 °C chamber temperature (thompson2026designanddevelopment pages 16-18). A minimum of four coats of the adhesive was recommended for best results, and a brim was still needed for most parts because warpage could occur even with properly applied adhesive (thompson2026designanddevelopment pages 16-18). The printer produced ULTEM 1010 calibration cubes (20 × 20 × 20 mm) and successful ULTEM 9085 and PEEK parts, confirming the suitability of this glass-plus-adhesive approach at high bed temperatures. The printer's heated bed could reach 200 °C and its chamber heater 120 °C (thompson2026designanddevelopment pages 16-18).

### 2.3 PEI (ULTEM) Sheet with Magigoo HT Adhesive

Magigoo HT, a commercial adhesive engineered for high-temperature polymers (PEEK, PEKK, PEI), was tested on a PEI build sheet for ULTEM 1000 printing at bed temperatures of 120, 150, and 180 °C (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 158-166, fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 215-223). The results were as follows:

- **120 °C bed**: Significant warping across the entire specimen; the adhesive and 10 mm brim were insufficient to keep the part flat, and warping began during deposition of the first layer (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 209-215, fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 215-223).
- **150 °C bed**: Dramatic improvement, with only slight warping at the extreme edges of the part, occurring mainly upon removal from the build surface due to residual stresses. During printing, adhesion was adequate and no warping occurred (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 215-223).
- **180 °C bed**: The part adhered perfectly with no significant warping, either during printing or after removal (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 215-223).

Magigoo HT provided adequate adhesion for complex and elongated geometries including tensile test specimens, where a previous attempt with Dimafix had failed (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 158-166, fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 174-181).

### 2.4 PEI Sheet with Dimafix Spray — Not Recommended

Dimafix spray adhesive, while effective for ABS at 120 °C bed temperature, degraded and lost its adhesive properties above approximately 125 °C (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 158-166). When used for ULTEM printing at 125 °C, it could not restrain high-shrinkage geometries such as tensile specimens, though shorter compression cylinders were successful. The limitation was attributed to the high thermal stresses generated by ULTEM's large extrusion-to-bed temperature gradient (350–400 °C vs. 125 °C) exceeding Dimafix's adhesive capacity (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 158-166, fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 174-181).

### 2.5 Sanded Carbon-Fibre Composite Plate

Initial PEI printing trials on a sanded 1.5 mm carbon-fibre surface at a 150 °C bed temperature showed good adhesion, with 1 mm-thick specimens exhibiting no visible warping or shrinkage after cooling (shuttleworth2020adigitalmanufacturing pages 71-75). However, the aluminium base plate supporting this surface buckled during heating, motivating the switch to borosilicate glass. The carbon-fibre surface's performance was validated only for thin parts, and no removal-force, wear, or lifetime data were reported.

### 2.6 PEI-Coated Spring Steel

Adhesion testing with PETG (not ULTEM) on PEI-coated spring steel yielded a mean maximum tear-off force of 53.48 ± 7.95 N, compared with only 33.09 ± 5.52 N on uncoated aluminium (kascak2024adhesiontestingdevice pages 8-9). The flexible spring steel sheet can be bent to aid part release after cooling. However, these measurements were performed with PETG at 85 °C and cannot be directly extrapolated to ULTEM at 150–200 °C. The PEI coating's T_g (~217 °C for ULTEM 1010) means that at high bed temperatures approaching or exceeding this value, the coating itself may soften and bond to the printed part, posing a fusion risk.

### 2.7 Bare Aluminium — Not Recommended

Aluminium exhibited thermal expansion problems at the temperatures required for PEI printing. A thin aluminium heated bed buckled during heating to 150 °C, producing approximately 1.5 mm of edge deviation and uneven part thickness (shuttleworth2020adigitalmanufacturing pages 71-75). Additionally, bare aluminium showed the lowest adhesion force in comparative testing (33.09 N mean for PETG) (kascak2024adhesiontestingdevice pages 8-9).

### 2.8 Bare Borosilicate Glass — Insufficient Without Adhesive

Smooth bare borosilicate glass was found to lose adhesion after the first few prints of a high-temperature thermoplastic polyimide; a PEI bed with nano polymer adhesive was subsequently adopted to address this problem (kothavade2024extrusion3dprinting pages 4-5). Similarly, PI tape and PVP adhesive were applied to glass because the smooth surface alone was insufficient for PEI adhesion (shuttleworth2020adigitalmanufacturing pages 71-75).

### 2.9 Stratasys Fortus/F900 Industrial Systems

Stratasys Fortus 450mc and F900 systems, the primary industrial platforms for ULTEM 9085 and 1010, employ maximum active-convection chamber temperatures of ≤220 °C and ≤225 °C, respectively (wratkowski2021acharacterizationof pages 4-6, wratkowski2021acharacterizationof pages 6-8). These systems use dual extrusion with breakaway or soluble support materials, and parts are printed on disposable build sheets with a machine-generated support-material foundation (raft) that mediates adhesion and release. While this approach is industrially validated and qualified for aerospace applications, the specific build sheet composition and bed temperature setpoints were not disclosed in the reviewed literature (wratkowski2021acharacterizationof pages 4-6). The disposable single-use build sheet avoids cumulative surface damage but adds per-build consumable cost.

### 2.10 G10/FR4 Garolite

G10/FR4 glass-epoxy laminate is mentioned in the context of large-format additive manufacturing systems, but no controlled ULTEM adhesion-force, release, or lifetime data were located in the reviewed literature. The principal concern is the limited thermal capability of the epoxy matrix: standard FR4 grades have T_g values in the 130–180 °C range, and prolonged exposure to PEI printing bed temperatures (150–200 °C) can cause discolouration, warping, or delamination of the laminate.

### 2.11 PEEK and PPSU Sheets

No controlled build-plate adhesion data for ULTEM printed on PEEK or PPSU sheets were identified in the reviewed literature. PEEK (T_g ≈ 143 °C, continuous use up to ~250 °C) and PPSU (T_g ≈ 220 °C) are thermally compatible candidates, and their immiscibility with PEI might reduce fusion risk relative to a PEI-on-PEI configuration. However, without published adhesion or release data, their ranking remains speculative.

## 3. The Role of Bed and Chamber Temperature

The fundamental finding from warpage studies is that bed temperature is the dominant factor controlling first-layer adhesion and warpage for PEI printing. The general principle established for FFF adhesion—that optimal adhesion occurs at a bed temperature slightly above the glass transition temperature of the printing material (spoerk2018effectofthe pages 1-3, spoerk2018effectofthe pages 4-5)—implies that PEI ideally requires a bed temperature of approximately 190–220 °C (above T_g) for best adhesion and minimum warpage. At 120 °C, significant warping occurred in all ULTEM specimens tested; at 150 °C, warping was dramatically reduced; and at 180 °C, warping was eliminated (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 215-223).

Chamber temperature provides a secondary but important benefit. A heated chamber reduces the thermal gradient between deposited layers and the environment, thereby reducing residual stresses. Increasing the heated chamber temperature from ambient to 120 °C produced a 36% reduction in warpage RMSD for PEI samples, though approximately 1 mm of deflection remained at specimen extremities (shuttleworth2020adigitalmanufacturinga pages 99-104, shuttleworth2020adigitalmanufacturing pages 99-104). PEI nozzle temperatures typically range from 355–390 °C, with bed temperatures of 120–160 °C and a heated chamber recommended (loh2020anoverviewof pages 4-5).

*Table: Ranked build-surface recommendations for temperature-limited and industrial high-temperature PEI/ULTEM printers. Ratings distinguish directly reported results from engineering extrapolations and identify important release and surface-damage risks.*

## 6. Summary and Conclusions

**For high-temperature printers (bed 160–200 °C, chamber ≥150 °C):** The best-supported approach is **borosilicate glass with a high-temperature adhesive** (Vision Miner Nano Polymer Adhesive or Magigoo HT), operated at the highest available bed temperature (ideally 180–200 °C). This combination provides strong adhesion without the risk of same-material fusion, the glass is dimensionally stable and reusable, and the adhesive coating is renewable. This was validated for ULTEM 1010 at a 200 °C bed (thompson2026designanddevelopment pages 16-18) and for ULTEM 1000 at 150–180 °C with Magigoo HT (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 215-223). Alternatively, borosilicate glass with PI tape and PVP adhesive is validated at 150 °C (shuttleworth2020adigitalmanufacturing pages 71-75) and offers a thermally robust interface. A PEI sheet with Magigoo HT is effective, particularly at 180 °C where warpage was eliminated (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 215-223), but users should be aware of the PEI-to-PEI fusion risk at higher temperatures.

**For temperature-limited printers (bed ~120 °C, chamber ~65 °C):** Printing PEI at these temperatures is inherently challenging because 120 °C is far below the T_g of either ULTEM grade. Significant warpage was documented at a 120 °C bed even with adhesive and brim (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 209-215, fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 215-223). The best compromise is **borosilicate glass with PI tape and Magigoo HT**, combined with a large brim (10–20 mm), slow first-layer speed (10 mm/s), and infrared preheating of the first layer if available (fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 158-166, fabrizio2020improvementofthermal pages 174-181). Users should expect partial warpage on larger parts and should consider printing only small or geometrically forgiving parts at this limited bed temperature.

**Surfaces to avoid for PEI printing** include bare aluminium (thermal distortion), bare borosilicate glass without adhesive (insufficient grip), Dimafix spray (degrades above ~125 °C), and uncoated PEI sheets at bed temperatures above ~200 °C (fusion risk). Standard PVA glue sticks are not rated for the temperatures involved and should not be used.

info.query: For material-extrusion (FFF/FDM) 3D printing of polyetherimide (PEI; SABIC ULTEM 9085 and ULTEM 1010 filament, Tg about 186 C and 217 C), which build plate (print bed) material and surface treatment gives the best first-layer adhesion during printing combined with clean, damage-free part release afterwards? Compare the candidate bed surfaces reported in the literature and in printer and material-supplier documentation: polyimide (Kapton) film or tape on glass or aluminium; borosilicate glass, bare or with adhesives (PVA glue stick, PEI/ULTEM dissolved in solvent as a slurry, commercial high-temperature adhesives such as Magigoo PEEK/PEI or Vision Miner Nano Polymer Adhesive); smooth or textured PEI (ULTEM) sheets, including the risk of a PEI part fusing to a PEI bed; G10/FR4 glass-epoxy (Garolite); PEEK or polysulfone/PPSU sheets; the high-temperature build sheets and support-material rafts used by Stratasys Fortus/F900 printers for ULTEM 9085 and ULTEM 1010; carbon-fibre composite plates; and bare or coated metal (aluminium, spring steel, steel with a PEI coating). For each surface report the bed and chamber temperatures used, measured adhesion force or warpage/curling, removal behaviour, surface wear or degradation and lifetime, and the maximum continuous-use temperature of the surface itself. Conclude with a ranked recommendation, and state separately what works best when the printer's bed is limited to about 120 C and its chamber to about 65 C, versus a printer with a 160-200 C bed and a heated chamber at 150 C or more.
